THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

There's a lot of speculation around an incoming SpaceX and Tesla merger

Here's 8 ways both companies BENEFIT IF it happens:

1. Investment-grade debt instead of private credit

$TSLA has $43.5B of cash and did $4.7B of operating cash flow last quarter. $SPCX is seeking $40B of debt just for NVIDIA chips and Morgan Stanley estimates it needs ~$84B of outside capital per YEAR through 2034

A combined company funds this with cash flow and investment-grade debt instead of private credit. Saving even 2-3 points of interest on $40B is $1B+ a year, and that compounds across the entire buildout

2. Starlink replaces cellular in every Tesla

Today, carriers collect an estimated $10/month per connected car, a large % of the total Tesla charges. Moving this in-house to Starlink not only means 100% of revenues moves in-house, but also a better product with (eventually) no dead zones

3. Starlink for Robotaxi and Humanoid Robots

Cybercabs are already getting built with Starlink inside them, a merger would mean this can come with no additional cost/sale required between the companies

4. Compute at cost and better optionality

Tesla has its own training compute today, which doubled in the first half of 2026, but FSD, Robotaxi and Optimus are only just getting started and they will need a LOT more compute

SpaceX is already building this out at size with 10GW expected by EOY 2027. Rather than leasing this to Tesla at market prices ($30M/MW ish right now), Tesla's extra demand can simply run on SpaceX compute at cost

SpaceX also now has more optionally with their compute. To move between leasing, using for Grok or now using for Tesla products

4. Energy at cost

Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage last quarter and xAI/SpaceX is one of Tesla's biggest customers ($430M of mostly Megapack revenue in 2025).

Merged, the data centers get Megapacks at cost with guaranteed supply, and yes, that intercompany revenue disappears in consolidation, but it's a wash since it's saved as an expense on the other side

5. Terafab gets built FASTER

Terafab today is a joint venture between two separately owned companies, so every major decision crosses two boards, two capital committees, and negotiated cost-sharing agreements.

Merged, one owner makes the call and capital moves the same day. Construction starts in December, and that speed advantage compounds through every phase after the first $16.8B. Elon's whole edge is iteration speed, and a JV structure is the opposite of that

6. Killing the duplicate overhead

Two public companies means two of everything: two legal departments, two HR orgs, two finance and audit functions, two IR teams, two procurement groups buying from the same suppliers.

Combined SG&A is about $11.2B. Cutting 15-25% of the ~$3.4B corporate slice of that is about $0.5-0.9B a year (est). Not the headline reason to merge, but still useful

SpaceX's AI buildout generated $3.7B of losses in the first half alone

Merged, those losses offset Tesla's taxable profit at the 21% corporate rate, worth roughly $0.3-1.0B a year

Though looks like SpaceX is soon going to generate a profit, so this may be irrelevant after next earnings

Tesla's fleet generates real-world data, X and Grok have additional data and SpaceX has its own data. Currently Tesla and SpaceX data are separate and have corporate boundaries and conflict disclosure issues

data.translation:
Elon Musk suggests not cooling chips for space, but rather letting them work hot.

Here’s the real paradox of space data centers.

Everyone thinks: “It’s −270 °C in space, chips will cool themselves.” In reality, it’s the opposite. In a vacuum, there’s no air or water to carry away heat. The vacuum acts like a giant thermos: the heat generated by the chip stays inside. The only way to get rid of it is to radiate it out as infrared light from large radiator panels.

And that’s where the harsh physics kicks in. The colder the radiator, the weaker it radiates. According to the Stefan–Boltzmann law, radiation power grows proportional to the **fourth power** of absolute temperature. If you raise the chip’s operating temperature by just 20% in kelvins, the radiators start emitting twice as much heat. That means they can be made twice as small and lighter.

That’s exactly what Musk is talking about in the video:  
“If you increase the operating temperature by 20% in kelvins, the mass of the radiators can be cut in half. That’s why it’s advantageous to operate at a higher temperature in space.”

On Earth, we spend billions to keep chips cold. In space, it’s more cost-effective to design chips that can comfortably run at 100–120 °C. Then the radiators become significantly lighter, and launch costs drop sharply. Plus, neural networks are quite resilient to random bit flips from radiation—for a massive model, a few flipped bits mean almost nothing.

So it turns out the main challenge for space AI isn’t energy (the sun in space is free and constant), but heat dissipation. And Musk proposes solving it not with cooling, but with temperature.

It seems almost counterintuitive, but the physics is on his side.

И тут начинается жёсткая физика. Чем холоднее радиатор, тем слабее он излучает. По закону Стефана–Больцмана мощность излучения растёт пропорционально **четвёртой степени** абсолютной температуры. Tesla presentó en Texas una demostración de su nuevo Roadster, un deportivo eléctrico que promete acelerar de 0 a 96 km/h en menos de un segundo, circular boca abajo y realizar saltos sobre otros vehículos. El modelo combina motores eléctricos de hasta 1.360 CV con propulsores de aire comprimido desarrollados junto a SpaceX. Su llegada al mercado está prevista para 2028.

Cómo funciona
El vehículo utiliza ventiladores bajo el piso para aumentar la adherencia y propulsores que expulsan aire comprimido para generar empuje adicional. Su tecnología incluye componentes derivados de los cohetes de SpaceX y motores del robot humanoide Optimus. La versión Rocket incorpora 10 propulsores direccionales que permiten elevar el auto, controlar sus movimientos en el aire y amortiguar los aterrizajes.

La limitación de 7 horas
El tanque de 200 litros de la versión Thrust se vacía en apenas seis segundos de funcionamiento a máxima potencia. La versión Rocket dispone de 600 litros de aire comprimido, cuya recarga mediante el compresor integrado demora entre seis y siete horas. Tesla trabaja para reducir ese tiempo a 30 minutos antes del lanzamiento comercial previsto para 2028.

Versiones
La gama incluirá una versión básica de 1.088 CV, con una autonomía estimada de entre 483 y 515 kilómetros; la Thrust, capaz de acelerar de 0 a 96 km/h en 0,8 segundos; y la Rocket, monoplaza, que promete hacerlo en 0,55 segundos y estará reservada a clientes seleccionados.

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
